intro.html: People handle money in very different ways, and English has a sharp word for each. Some save every penny, some spend as if the money will never run out, some give it away by the bagful, and some want it all for themselves.

Sort the ten words into four groups. Savers: frugal (wise), parsimonious (stingy), avaricious (greedy). Spenders: extravagant, prodigal, profligate (each more wasteful than the last). Givers: munificent, largesse. Rich and poor: affluent, destitute.
Notice which words praise and which ones criticize. Calling a friend frugal is a compliment; calling him parsimonious is not, even though both describe a person who spends little.

words.def: careful not to waste money, food or other things; thrifty
words.ex: Our {frugal} grandmother saves twist ties, rubber bands and every jar that still has a lid.
words.ctx: Though the family had plenty of money, they stayed {frugal}: they mended old clothes, grew their own beans and rarely ate at restaurants.
words.etym: From Latin frugalis, “thrifty, simple,” from frux (fruit, the produce of the land).

mn.text: Nana Lou saves every coin, even the one she found under the sofa cushion, and patches her coat instead of buying a new one; she is {frugal}.

scene.alt: Nana Lou holds up a coin she found by the sofa, ready to drop it into her piggy bank.

words.def: so unwilling to spend money that one is stingy
words.ex: The {parsimonious} landlord would not even replace the burned-out light in the stairwell.
words.ctx: The club’s treasurer was so {parsimonious} that she refused to buy new soccer balls, even after the old ones had gone flat and split at the seams.
words.etym: From parsimony, from Latin parsimonia, “thrift,” from parcere (to spare).

mn.text: Look inside the word and you will find Simon, who hugs his money bag and will not chip in even a penny for the class party; Simon is {parsimonious}.

scene.alt: A stingy man named Simon hugs his money bag and refuses to add a penny to a girl’s party jar.

words.def: spending far more than is wise or needed; going beyond reason
words.ex: For her dog’s birthday, Mrs. Hale threw an {extravagant} party with a three-layer cake and a hired band.
words.ctx: Their first apartment was tiny and cheap, so a piano that cost more than a year’s rent seemed {extravagant} to everyone they knew.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin extravagans, “wandering beyond (the limits)”: extra- (beyond) + vagari (to wander).
words.note: Extravagant can describe more than spending: extravagant praise or extravagant claims go far beyond what is reasonable.

mn.text: Mrs. Hale buys an extra cake, extra balloons and an extra band for her dog’s party, just because; spending that far beyond what makes sense is {extravagant}.

scene.alt: A woman in a party hat cheers at her dog’s birthday, surrounded by two cakes, balloons and gifts.

words.def: carelessly wasteful with money or other resources
words.ex: The {prodigal} young heir spent his whole fortune on racehorses in a single year.
words.ctx: Having been {prodigal} with his allowance all summer, buying every comic and candy bar in sight, Jonah had nothing left when the county fair finally came to town.
words.etym: From Latin prodigus, “wasteful,” from prodigere, “to drive away, to squander”: pro- (forth) + agere (to drive).
words.note: Prodigal means wasteful. A famous story tells of a prodigal son who wasted his money and then came home, so people sometimes use the word for anyone returning, but returning is not its meaning.

mn.cue: PROD the GOLD out the door
mn.text: Rich Rosa prods her gold coins right out the door with a broom, spending on anything that glitters; anyone that wasteful is {prodigal}.

scene.alt: A young woman in a tiara laughs as she sweeps a pile of gold coins out the open door.

words.ex: The {profligate} prince spent the royal treasury on golden fountains while the town’s roads crumbled.
words.ctx: The company’s {profligate} spending, on private jets and lavish parties, left it unable to pay its workers when sales slowed.
words.etym: From Latin profligatus, past participle of profligare (to strike down, to ruin).
words.note: Profligate can also describe someone who lives wildly, with no self-control; as a noun, a profligate is a reckless spender.

mn.text: Rex flings handfuls of gold coins off the bridge just to hear them splash; spending money that recklessly is {profligate}.

scene.alt: A man in a top hat tosses gold coins off a bridge into the river while a duck stares in shock.

words.ex: Thanks to a {munificent} gift from a former student, the school built a new music hall.
words.ctx: Most guests brought a small present, but Aunt Rosa was {munificent}: she paid for the whole wedding dinner and the band as well.

mn.cue: MOON-IF-icent: he’d give you the MOON
mn.text: Uncle Omar would give you the moon if he could; he has already paid for the whole team’s trip. He is {munificent}.

scene.alt: A generous uncle holds up the moon itself as a gift while two children cheer.

words.def: generous giving, or the gifts given
words.ex: Every December the baker’s {largesse} filled the shelter’s tables with bread and pies.
words.ctx: The tiny library survived on the {largesse} of one devoted reader, who paid for new books every year and asked for nothing in return.
words.etym: From French largesse, from large (generous, open-handed).
words.note: Also spelled largesse, the more common spelling today.

mn.text: From the castle wall, the queen tosses down a large sack of bread and coins for the whole village; generous giving that large is {largesse}.

scene.alt: A queen hands out a big sack of coins and bread to cheering villagers.

words.ex: The {avaricious} dragon slept on a mountain of gold and counted every coin each morning.
words.ctx: Rex was so {avaricious} that he charged his own brother for a cup of water and hoarded his gold rather than buy himself a winter coat.
words.etym: From avarice, from Latin avaritia (greed), from avarus (greedy).

mn.cue: HAVE-a-RICH-us: I must HAVE all the RICHES
mn.text: The dragon must have all the riches in the land and growls at anyone who comes near its pile; it is {avaricious}.

scene.alt: A greedy dragon guards a treasure chest, coins, gems and a crown in its cave.

words.ex: The {affluent} family spent every summer at their lake house.
words.ctx: The fishing village was once poor, but after the harbor was rebuilt it grew {affluent}: new houses lined the hill and sailboats crowded the docks.
words.etym: From Latin affluere, “to flow toward, to abound”: ad- (to) + fluere (to flow).

mn.text: For the Hills family, money flows in like a river; they are {affluent}.

scene.alt: A rich man in a top hat holds up a bucket as gold coins pour down from a cloud.

words.def: without money, a home or the basic things needed to live
words.ex: After the flood, many {destitute} families slept in the school gym until their homes could be rebuilt.
words.ctx: Once a wealthy merchant, he lost all his ships in a single storm and was left {destitute}, with no house, no savings and only the coat on his back.
words.etym: From Latin destitutus, “abandoned,” from destituere (to forsake, to leave without).

mn.text: After the storm sank his ship, the merchant had not a stitch to his name but the shirt he wore; he was {destitute}.

scene.alt: A shipwrecked merchant sits on the beach holding an empty wallet beside broken planks.

head: word
who it describes
praise or blame?
after.cap: Savers, spenders and givers: the same habit can earn praise or blame.

after.html: Largess (also spelled largesse) is the noun for what a munificent person gives. Affluent and destitute sit at the two ends of having: plenty and nothing.

items.q: True or false: prodigal means “returning home after a long time away.”
items.why: False. Prodigal means wasteful. A well-known story is about a prodigal son who came home, which is why people mix them up.

items.q: Which word would you use to praise someone who spends carefully?
items.why: Frugal is a compliment: careful and thrifty. Parsimonious means stingy, and avaricious means greedy.

items.q: In affluent, the root flu (as in fluid) means…
items.why: flu means flow: an affluent family has money flowing in.

items.q: The retired teacher paid for every student’s field trip and bought the class a new microscope. She was…
items.why: Giving that freely and lavishly is munificent.
